items.title: Nature & Scope of Science, Technology and Innovation
items.body:
### Science, technology and innovation

**In one line**
Science is knowing *why*, technology is using that knowledge to *do* something, and innovation is getting that something *actually used* by people or the market.

**The story**
These three words are often blurred, but APPSC tests the difference. **Science** is the systematic search for knowledge about the natural world through observation, experiment and reasoning — it answers 'how does nature work?'. **Technology** takes that knowledge and applies it to build tools, processes and products that solve real problems. **Innovation** goes one step further: it is the *successful introduction* of a new or improved product, process or service into use or the market. The key insight is that an **invention** (a new idea or device) only becomes an **innovation** when it is adopted and creates value — a brilliant device locked in a lab is an invention, not an innovation.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Statement-based MCQs regularly ask you to sort these definitions and to spot the trap 'invention = innovation'. The theme also underpins Mains answers on India becoming an innovation-led economy.

**Picture it**

| Term | Core idea | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| Science | knowledge of the natural world | understanding how a virus spreads |
| Technology | applying that knowledge | designing a vaccine |
| Innovation | successful real-world use | mass-producing and delivering the vaccine via a cold chain |

**Terms explained**
- **Scientific temper** — a rational, evidence-based, questioning attitude rather than belief in superstition or dogma.
- **STI** — Science, Technology and Innovation, treated together as an engine of growth.
- **Atmanirbhar Bharat** — the self-reliant-India vision that STI is meant to serve.

**Scientific temper and the Constitution**
- **Article 51A(h)** makes it a **Fundamental Duty** of every citizen to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. It was inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**, and the phrase was popularised by Nehru. India is among the very few countries to mention scientific temper in its Constitution.

**Don't confuse**
- **Invention vs innovation** — invention creates; innovation adopts and adds value.
- **Article 51A(h) vs 51A(g)** — (h) is scientific temper; (g) is protecting the natural environment.

**Remember it**
"Know it (Science) → Build it (Technology) → Use it widely (Innovation)."

**TL;DR**
- Science = knowledge of nature; Technology = applying it; Innovation = successful real-world use.
- Invention is not innovation — innovation needs adoption and value.
- Article 51A(h) makes scientific temper a Fundamental Duty (42nd Amendment, 1976).
- STI drives Atmanirbhar Bharat and everyday services (health, agriculture, UPI).
keyPoints: Science = knowledge of the natural world; Technology = applying that knowledge; Innovation = successful real-world use of a new/improved product or process.
Invention is not the same as innovation — innovation requires adoption/value.
Article 51A(h) makes developing scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry a Fundamental Duty.
Fundamental Duties (incl. 51A(h)) were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
STI drives Atmanirbhar Bharat and everyday services like health, agriculture and UPI.
items.mnemonic: Know it (Science) -> Build it (Technology) -> Use it widely (Innovation).
items.source: DST STI policy framework; Constitution of India Article 51A(h)

items.title: Evolution of India's S&T Policy (1958 to draft 2020)
items.body:
### How India's science policy evolved

**In one line**
India's science policy grew in five steps — from simply building scientific capacity in 1958 to an inclusive, innovation-led vision in the 2020 draft.

**The story**
At independence the priority was to *create* science: the **Scientific Policy Resolution (SPR) 1958** under Nehru set out to cultivate science and scientific temper and bring its benefits to the people, building bodies like CSIR and DAE. By the 1980s the worry was import-dependence, so the **Technology Policy Statement (TPS) 1983** under Indira Gandhi pushed **technological self-reliance** and indigenous capability. The **Science and Technology Policy (STP) 2003** under Vajpayee integrated science with technology, called for higher investment and linked S&T to equity. The landmark **Science, Technology and Innovation Policy (STIP) 2013** added the word **'Innovation'** to the title for the first time, adopted the theme 'STI for the People', and aimed to make India a top-five scientific power with a **2% GERD** goal. The **draft STIP 2020**, prepared by the Office of the PSA and DST through a decentralised, bottom-up consultation, would be the fifth policy — but it remains un-notified as of 2026.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Match-the-policy-to-the-year and 'which policy first used Innovation' are frequent MCQs; the shift in emphasis is a ready-made Mains answer.

**Picture it**

| Policy | Year | Era | Thrust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scientific Policy Resolution (SPR) | 1958 | Nehru | cultivate science & scientific temper |
| Technology Policy Statement (TPS) | 1983 | Indira Gandhi | technological self-reliance |
| Science & Technology Policy (STP) | 2003 | Vajpayee | integrate S&T; raise investment; equity |
| Science, Technology & Innovation Policy (STIP) | 2013 | Manmohan Singh | 'STI for the People'; top-5; 2% GERD |
| Draft STIP | 2020 | — | decentralised, bottom-up; still a draft |

**Terms explained**
- **GERD** — Gross Expenditure on Research and Development, measured as a share of GDP.
- **Notified** — formally adopted and brought into force by the government (the 2020 draft is not yet notified).

**Don't confuse**
- **STP 2003 vs STIP 2013** — 'Innovation' entered the title only in 2013, not 2003.
- **Adopted vs draft** — four policies are adopted (1958, 1983, 2003, 2013); STIP 2020 is only a draft.

**Remember it**
Policy order by last digit of the year: **58 → 83 → 03 → 13 → (20 draft)**.

**TL;DR**
- Four adopted S&T policies: SPR 1958, TPS 1983, STP 2003, STIP 2013; STIP 2020 is a draft.
- SPR 1958 stressed scientific temper; TPS 1983 stressed self-reliance.
- 'Innovation' entered the title only with STIP 2013, which set the 2% GERD and top-5 goals.
- Draft STIP 2020 (PSA + DST) is decentralised/bottom-up and not yet notified; real GERD is only about 0.64%.
keyPoints: Four adopted S&T policies: SPR 1958, TPS 1983, STP 2003, STIP 2013; STIP 2020 is a draft.
SPR 1958 (Nehru) stressed scientific temper; TPS 1983 stressed technological self-reliance.
'Innovation' entered the policy title only with STIP 2013.
STIP 2013 aimed to put India among the top 5 scientific powers and raise GERD to 2% of GDP.
Draft STIP 2020 (PSA + DST) is decentralised/bottom-up and not yet notified.
items.mnemonic: Policy order 'S-T-S-S' years 58-83-03-13 (SPR, TPS, STP, STIP).
items.source: DST (dst.gov.in) — evolution of S&T policy; draft STIP 2020

items.title: Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), 2023
items.body:
### The apex research-funding body

**In one line**
The ANRF is India's new top body to fund and steer research, created in 2023 to pull in private money and replace the older SERB.

**The story**
For years India's research funding was spread thinly and leaned almost entirely on the government. To fix this, Parliament passed the **Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act, 2023**, setting up the ANRF as the **apex body** to fund, coordinate and promote research across natural sciences, technology, agriculture, health and allied fields. It **subsumed the Science and Engineering Research Board (SERB)** (set up in 2008). What makes the ANRF distinctive is its funding model: of an envisaged **Rs 50,000 crore over 2023-28**, a large share — about **Rs 36,000 crore** — is expected from **industry and philanthropy**, a deliberate push to raise the low private share in research. Its **Governing Board is chaired by the Prime Minister** as ex-officio President, with the Union Ministers of Science & Technology and Education as Vice-Presidents, and it aligns with the National Education Policy 2020. PM Modi chaired its first Governing Board meeting in September 2024.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'ANRF replaced which body?', its PM-chaired board, and the private-funding target are high-frequency current-affairs MCQs.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Set up by | ANRF Act, 2023 |
| Replaced | SERB (2008) |
| Outlay | ~Rs 50,000 crore (2023-28) |
| Private share | ~Rs 36,000 crore from industry/philanthropy |
| Chair | Prime Minister (ex-officio President) |

**Terms explained**
- **Apex body** — the highest coordinating/funding authority in its field.
- **Ex-officio** — holding a position automatically by virtue of another office (the PM chairs it by being PM).
- **SERB** — the Science and Engineering Research Board, the earlier grant-giving body now merged into ANRF.

**Don't confuse**
- **ANRF vs RDI Scheme** — ANRF (2023) is the apex funding foundation; the RDI Scheme (2025) is a separate financing scheme that complements, not replaces, it.
- **ANRF under DST, not Home** — it functions under the Department of Science and Technology.

**Remember it**
"**A**NRF **A**bsorbed SERB, **A**ims to attract private money, **A**pex and PM-led."

**TL;DR**
- ANRF was created under the ANRF Act, 2023 and replaced SERB (2008).
- It is the apex body funding research across sciences, technology, agriculture and health.
- Outlay ~Rs 50,000 crore (2023-28), ~Rs 36,000 crore from private/non-government sources.
- The Prime Minister is ex-officio President of its Governing Board; first meeting Sept 2024.
keyPoints: ANRF was created under the ANRF Act, 2023 and replaced the SERB (2008).
It is the apex body funding research in natural sciences, technology, agriculture and health.
Outlay about Rs 50,000 crore over 2023-28, with about Rs 36,000 crore expected from private/non-government sources.
The Prime Minister is ex-officio President of its Governing Board.
It advances the NEP 2020 vision of a research-led ecosystem; first Board meeting held Sept 2024.
items.source: Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act, 2023; PIB

items.title: Key S&T Institutions & Administrative Structure
items.body:
### Who runs science in India

**In one line**
India's science is run by a Ministry of Science and Technology with three departments, plus powerful stand-alone bodies like the DAE and ISRO that report elsewhere.

**The story**
The **Ministry of Science and Technology** has three departments: **DST** (1971), which promotes and coordinates S&T and runs most schemes; **DBT** (1986) for biotechnology; and **DSIR**, which handles industrial research and is the parent of **CSIR**. CSIR (founded 1942) is one of the world's largest publicly funded R&D networks, running about **37 laboratories** such as NPL and NCL. Crucially, some strategic bodies sit *outside* this ministry: the **Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)** (1954), associated with **Homi J. Bhabha**, works **directly under the Prime Minister**; BARC (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre), IGCAR (Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research) and NPCIL are among its constituent units; **ISRO** works under the Department of Space. Advice flows through the **Principal Scientific Adviser (PSA)**, who chairs the **PM's Science, Technology and Innovation Advisory Council (PM-STIAC)**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
APPSC asks which bodies belong to the Ministry (DAE is a trap — it does not), establishment years, and who the PSA is.

**Picture it**

| Body | Year | Reports to | Mandate |
|---|---|---|---|
| DST | 1971 | Ministry of S&T | promote/coordinate S&T |
| DBT | 1986 | Ministry of S&T | biotechnology |
| DSIR / CSIR | 1942 (CSIR) | Ministry of S&T | industrial research; 37 labs |
| DAE | 1954 | Prime Minister | atomic energy (BARC, IGCAR, NPCIL) |
| ISRO | 1969 | Dept of Space | space |

**Terms explained**
- **CSIR** — Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, the national lab network under DSIR.
- **PSA** — Principal Scientific Adviser, the government's top science adviser.
- **PM-STIAC** — the PM's advisory council on science missions, chaired by the PSA.

**Don't confuse**
- **DAE is NOT in the Ministry of S&T** — it reports directly to the PM.
- **PSA does not head DST** — DST is run by its Secretary; the PSA is an adviser.
- **ICMR/ICAR/DRDO/ISRO** are apex bodies but sit under health, agriculture, defence and space respectively.

**Remember it**
"The Ministry's three D's = **DST, DBT, DSIR**; DAE is the odd one out — under the PM."

**TL;DR**
- Ministry of Science & Technology has three departments: DST (1971), DBT (1986), DSIR.
- CSIR (1942) works under DSIR and runs about 37 laboratories.
- DAE (1954) functions directly under the PM and is linked to Homi Bhabha (BARC, IGCAR, NPCIL).
- ICMR, ICAR, DRDO and ISRO are other apex bodies; the PSA chairs PM-STIAC.
keyPoints: Ministry of Science & Technology has three departments: DST (1971), DBT (1986) and DSIR.
CSIR (1942) works under DSIR and runs about 37 laboratories.
DAE (1954) functions directly under the PM and is linked to Homi J. Bhabha (BARC, IGCAR, NPCIL).
ICMR (medical), ICAR (agriculture), DRDO (defence) and ISRO (space) are other apex S&T bodies.
The PSA advises the government and chairs PM-STIAC; DST is headed by its Secretary, not the PSA.

Numbers to remember: ISRO 1969 under the Department of Space; NM-ICPS has set up 25 Technology Innovation Hubs; of the ANRF outlay about Rs 36,000 crore is expected from industry and philanthropy; India ranked 38th in the Global Innovation Index 2025.
items.mnemonic: Ministry's three D's = DST, DBT, DSIR (DAE is separate, under the PM).

items.title: Mission-Mode S&T Initiatives
items.body:
### India's deep-tech missions

**In one line**
Mission-mode programmes pour focused money into deep-tech — quantum, supercomputing, cyber-physical systems — and try to pull in private investment to lift India's low research spend.

**The story**
Rather than scatter funds, the government launches time-bound **missions** aimed at strategic technologies. The **National Quantum Mission**, approved by the Union Cabinet in **2023** and implemented by the **Department of Science and Technology (DST)**, has a total outlay of **Rs 6003.65 crore** (2023-24 to 2030-31) across four thematic hubs in computing, communication, sensing and materials. The **National Supercomputing Mission (2015)** builds indigenous **PARAM** supercomputers (such as PARAM Rudra) through C-DAC. **NM-ICPS (2018)**, with about Rs 3,660 crore, targets Cyber-Physical Systems and has set up **25 Technology Innovation Hubs**. The newest, the **RDI Scheme (2025)**, carries a corpus of about **Rs 1 lakh crore** to give long-tenure, low-cost finance to **private-sector R&D** in sunrise and strategic sectors. These missions aim at strategic autonomy and at crowding in private money to raise India's low GERD; the RDI Scheme complements — it does not replace — the ANRF.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Mission names, years, outlays (especially the quantum figure) and 'which mission does what' matches are standard current-affairs items.

**Picture it**

| Mission | Year | Scale | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Quantum Mission | 2023 | Rs 6003.65 cr | quantum computing/communication/sensing (4 hubs) |
| National Supercomputing Mission | 2015 | — | PARAM supercomputers via C-DAC |
| NM-ICPS | 2018 | ~Rs 3,660 cr | Cyber-Physical Systems; 25 innovation hubs |
| RDI Scheme | 2025 | ~Rs 1 lakh crore | low-cost finance for private-sector R&D |

**Terms explained**
- **Deep-tech** — advanced, science-heavy technologies (quantum, AI, advanced materials).
- **Cyber-Physical Systems** — systems linking computation with physical processes (robotics, smart grids).
- **GERD** — Gross Expenditure on R&D as a share of GDP.

**Don't confuse**
- **RDI Scheme vs ANRF** — RDI (2025) finances private R&D; ANRF (2023) is the apex funding foundation; they complement each other.
- **Supercomputing (PARAM) vs Quantum Mission** — PARAM is classical supercomputing; the Quantum Mission builds quantum machines.

**Remember it**
"**Q**uantum = **6,000-odd** crore; **RDI** = **1 lakh** crore for private R&D."

**TL;DR**
- National Quantum Mission (2023): Rs 6003.65 crore, 2023-24 to 2030-31, four hubs.
- National Supercomputing Mission delivers indigenous PARAM supercomputers via C-DAC.
- NM-ICPS (2018) focuses on Cyber-Physical Systems and set up 25 Technology Innovation Hubs.
- RDI Scheme (2025): ~Rs 1 lakh crore to finance private-sector R&D; complements ANRF.
keyPoints: National Quantum Mission (2023): Rs 6003.65 crore, 2023-24 to 2030-31, four thematic hubs.
National Supercomputing Mission delivers indigenous PARAM supercomputers via C-DAC.
NM-ICPS (2018) focuses on Cyber-Physical Systems and set up 25 Technology Innovation Hubs.
RDI Scheme (2025): about Rs 1 lakh crore corpus to finance private-sector R&D in sunrise sectors.
RDI Scheme complements ANRF; both aim to raise India's low GERD.
items.source: PIB — National Quantum Mission, RDI Scheme; DST — NSM, NM-ICPS

items.title: R&D Spend, Innovation Ranking & Recent Initiatives
items.body:
### How much India spends and how it ranks

**In one line**
India spends only about 0.64% of GDP on research — far short of its 2% goal — yet keeps climbing the global innovation table through new access and funding schemes.

**The story**
A country's research effort is measured by **GERD** — Gross Expenditure on R&D as a share of GDP. India's GERD is about **0.64%**, well below the STIP target of **2%** and behind China (about 2.4%) and the USA. A peculiar feature is that the **government funds most of it**, while the private share is low — the very gap ANRF and the RDI Scheme try to close. Despite low spend, India has risen steadily on the **Global Innovation Index (GII)**, published yearly by the **World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO)**: **39th in 2024** and **38th in 2025**, consistently topping the lower-middle-income group and the Central & Southern Asia region. Two recent enablers stand out: **One Nation One Subscription (ONOS)**, operational from **1 January 2025** via the INFLIBNET Centre (UGC), giving institutions centrally funded access to thousands of e-journals; and **Vigyan Dhara (2024)**, a unified DST scheme merging three umbrella schemes.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The GERD figure, 'who publishes the GII', India's current GII rank, and ONOS/Vigyan Dhara are frequent current-affairs MCQs.

**Picture it**

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| India's GERD | ~0.64% of GDP (target 2%) |
| GII publisher | WIPO |
| GII rank 2024 → 2025 | 39th → 38th |
| ONOS | operational 1 Jan 2025 (INFLIBNET/UGC) |
| Vigyan Dhara | 2024 DST scheme merger |

**Terms explained**
- **GERD** — total spending on R&D as a percentage of GDP.
- **GII** — Global Innovation Index, an annual ranking of countries by innovation performance.
- **WIPO** — World Intellectual Property Organization, the UN agency that publishes the GII.
- **INFLIBNET** — the UGC's Information and Library Network Centre that runs ONOS.

**Don't confuse**
- **GERD vs GII** — GERD is money spent (an input); GII is a ranking of innovation outcomes.
- **Who publishes the GII** — WIPO, not the World Bank or WEF.

**Remember it**
"India spends little (**0.64%**) but ranks well (**38th**) — effort gap, outcome gain."

**TL;DR**
- India's GERD is about 0.64% of GDP, well short of the 2% aspiration; government funds most of it.
- The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO; India was 39th (2024) and 38th (2025).
- India tops the lower-middle-income group in the GII.
- ONOS (from 1 Jan 2025, via INFLIBNET/UGC) and Vigyan Dhara (2024 DST merger) are recent enablers.
keyPoints: India's GERD is about 0.64% of GDP, well short of the 2% aspiration.
Government funds most R&D in India; the private-sector share is comparatively low.
The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO; India was 39th (2024) and 38th (2025).
India tops the lower-middle-income group in the GII.
ONOS (operational 1 Jan 2025, via INFLIBNET/UGC) and Vigyan Dhara (2024 DST scheme merger) are recent enablers.
items.source: DST R&D Statistics; WIPO GII 2024/2025; PIB — ONOS, Vigyan Dhara

items.title: Science & Technology Institutions in Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
### AP's science and technology map

**In one line**
After the 2014 bifurcation, Andhra Pradesh kept its spaceport and atmospheric lab and gained a cluster of new national institutes — while the big Hyderabad labs stayed in Telangana.

**The story**
AP's science backbone starts with space: the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR), Sriharikota** is ISRO's **primary spaceport**, launching PSLV, GSLV and LVM3 rockets. Nearby at **Gadanki** is the **National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL)**, an autonomous institute of the Department of Space for atmospheric and radar science. Because the richest national labs — the **Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB)**, IICT and NGRI — sat in Hyderabad and went to **Telangana** after 2014, AP built a fresh cluster of premier institutes: **IIT Tirupati, IISER Tirupati, NIT Andhra Pradesh (Tadepalligudem), IIPE Visakhapatnam** and **AIIMS Mangalagiri**. Looking ahead, the planned **Amaravati Quantum Valley** is being developed in the Amaravati capital region as a hub for quantum-computing research and industry; global technology firms such as IBM, TCS and L&T are associated with the project.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
APPSC loves location-matching and the classic trap 'is CCMB in AP?' (no — it is in Hyderabad, Telangana).

**Picture it**

| Institution | Location in AP |
|---|---|
| SDSC-SHAR (spaceport) | Sriharikota |
| NARL (atmospheric) | Gadanki, near Tirupati |
| IIT Tirupati | Yerpedu, Tirupati |
| IISER Tirupati | Tirupati |
| NIT Andhra Pradesh | Tadepalligudem (West Godavari) |
| IIPE (petroleum & energy) | Visakhapatnam |
| AIIMS | Mangalagiri (near Guntur) |
| Amaravati Quantum Valley | Amaravati (planned) |

**Terms explained**
- **Spaceport** — a site from which rockets are launched (Sriharikota is India's main one).
- **Autonomous institute** — a body funded by a department (here the Department of Space) but self-governing.
- **Bifurcation** — the 2014 split of united Andhra Pradesh into AP and Telangana.

**Don't confuse**
- **In AP vs in Telangana** — SDSC-SHAR, NARL, IIT/IISER Tirupati are in AP; **CCMB, IICT, NGRI are in Hyderabad (Telangana)**.
- **IIPE vs AIIMS** — IIPE is at Visakhapatnam (energy); AIIMS is at Mangalagiri (medical).

**Remember it**
AP tech map: "Sriharikota (space), Tirupati (IIT+IISER+NARL), Vizag (IIPE), Tadepalligudem (NIT), Mangalagiri (AIIMS), Amaravati (Quantum)".

**TL;DR**
- SDSC-SHAR (Sriharikota) is ISRO's primary spaceport; NARL is at Gadanki near Tirupati.
- Tirupati hosts both an IIT (Yerpedu) and an IISER.
- NIT AP is at Tadepalligudem; IIPE at Visakhapatnam; AIIMS at Mangalagiri.
- Amaravati Quantum Valley is a planned quantum hub; CCMB, IICT and NGRI are in Hyderabad (Telangana), not AP.
keyPoints: SDSC-SHAR (Sriharikota) is ISRO's primary spaceport; NARL is at Gadanki near Tirupati.
Tirupati hosts both an IIT (Yerpedu) and an IISER.
NIT Andhra Pradesh is at Tadepalligudem; IIPE is at Visakhapatnam; AIIMS is at Mangalagiri.
Amaravati Quantum Valley is a planned quantum-computing hub in AP's capital region.
CCMB, IICT and NGRI are in Hyderabad (Telangana), NOT Andhra Pradesh.
items.mnemonic: AP tech map: Sriharikota (space), Tirupati (IIT+IISER+NARL), Vizag (IIPE), Tadepalligudem (NIT), Mangalagiri (AIIMS), Amaravati (Quantum).
items.source: ISRO SDSC-SHAR; NARL; IIT Tirupati; IISER Tirupati; NIT AP; IIPE; AIIMS Mangalagiri; Govt of AP (Amaravati Quantum Valley)

items.title: Research Institutes & Laboratories — Where They Are
items.body:
## India's research map: institute → city

**In one line:** the big national laboratories (CSIR, DAE, ICMR, ICAR and DST bodies) each sit in a fixed city, and "institute → location" matching is a favourite exam format.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC and other PSCs ask "CFTRI is located at?", "which lab keeps Indian Standard Time?", "PRL Ahmedabad was founded by?" and the Hyderabad-vs-AP trap (CCMB, IICT, NGRI are in Telangana).

**The story**

CSIR (1942) built a chain of specialised laboratories after independence — food at Mysuru, leather at Chennai, drugs at Lucknow, the ocean at Goa. Pioneering scientists founded others: **Jamsetji Tata**'s vision produced the **Indian Institute of Science (1909)**, **Homi Bhabha** founded **TIFR (1945)**, **Vikram Sarabhai** founded the **Physical Research Laboratory (1947)**, **C.V. Raman** set up the **Raman Research Institute (1948)** and **J.C. Bose** the **Bose Institute (1917)**. Hyderabad became a major science city with CCMB, IICT, NGRI, CDFD, NIN, INCOIS and ICRISAT — all in Telangana after 2014.

### CSIR laboratories

| Laboratory | Location |
|---|---|
| **National Physical Laboratory (NPL) — keeper of Indian Standard Time** | New Delhi |
| **National Chemical Laboratory (NCL)** | Pune |
| **Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI)** | Lucknow |
| **Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI)** | Mysuru |
| **Central Leather Research Institute (CLRI)** | Chennai |
| **National Institute of Oceanography (NIO)** | Dona Paula, Goa |
| **National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI)** | Nagpur |
| **National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL) — Hansa and Saras aircraft** | Bengaluru |
| **Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (IICT)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **National Geophysical Research Institute (NGRI)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI)** | Karaikudi (Tamil Nadu) |
| **Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants (CIMAP)** | Lucknow |
| **Central Building Research Institute (CBRI)** | Roorkee |
| **Central Scientific Instruments Organisation (CSIO)** | Chandigarh |
| **Central Road Research Institute (CRRI)** | New Delhi |

### Other national research institutes

| Institute (founder / year) | Location |
|---|---|
| **Indian Institute of Science (1909; vision of Jamsetji Tata)** | Bengaluru |
| **Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (1945; Homi Bhabha)** | Mumbai |
| **Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)** | Trombay, Mumbai |
| **Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR)** | Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu) |
| **Physical Research Laboratory (1947; Vikram Sarabhai)** | Ahmedabad |
| **Raman Research Institute (1948; C.V. Raman)** | Bengaluru |
| **Bose Institute (1917; J.C. Bose)** | Kolkata |
| **Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (1876; Mahendralal Sircar) — where Raman discovered the Raman effect** | Kolkata |
| **Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics** | Kolkata |
| **National Institute of Virology (ICMR)** | Pune |
| **National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD)** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) — tsunami early warning** | Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **ICRISAT (dryland crops research)** | Patancheru, near Hyderabad (Telangana) |
| **Indian Agricultural Research Institute (Pusa Institute, ICAR)** | New Delhi |
| **Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences (ARIES)** | Nainital |
| **Indian Institute of Astrophysics (runs the Kodaikanal observatory)** | Bengaluru |

## Don't confuse
- **Hyderabad is in Telangana:** CCMB, IICT, NGRI, CDFD, NIN, INCOIS and ICRISAT are **not** in Andhra Pradesh.
- **Two Lucknow labs:** CDRI (drugs) and CIMAP (medicinal plants).
- **Three Bengaluru bodies:** IISc, NAL and the Raman Research Institute.
- **PRL Ahmedabad (Sarabhai) vs TIFR Mumbai (Bhabha).**

**Remember it:** "Food–Mysuru, Leather–Chennai, Drugs–Lucknow, Ocean–Goa, Time–Delhi (NPL)."

**TL;DR**
- NPL New Delhi keeps Indian Standard Time; CFTRI Mysuru; CLRI Chennai; CDRI Lucknow; NIO Goa.
- IISc Bengaluru (1909, Tata); TIFR Mumbai (1945, Bhabha); PRL Ahmedabad (1947, Sarabhai).
- Raman discovered his effect at IACS Kolkata (founded 1876 by Mahendralal Sircar).
keyPoints: National Physical Laboratory (NPL) — keeper of Indian Standard Time — New Delhi.
Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) — Lucknow.
Indian Institute of Science (1909; vision of Jamsetji Tata) — Bengaluru.
Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (1945; Homi Bhabha) — Mumbai.

items.title: Apex S&T Bodies, Science Advisers, Science Days & Awards
items.body:
## The apex bodies and the calendar of science

**In one line:** each sector has its own apex research council under a different ministry, the PSA advises the government, and three national days celebrate Indian science.

**Why it is asked:** "ICMR was set up in?", "DRDO is under which ministry?", "National Science Day is celebrated on?" and "who was India's first Principal Scientific Adviser?" are frequent MCQs.

**The story**

Medicine got the first research council — the body that became the **ICMR** began in **1911** as the Indian Research Fund Association. Agriculture followed with the **ICAR (1929)**, defence with the **DRDO (1958)** and space with **ISRO (1969)**, which the **Department of Space (1972)** controls. The **Ministry of Earth Sciences (2006)** runs weather and ocean bodies such as the **IMD (1875)**. The office of **Principal Scientific Adviser** began in **1999** with **A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**. India celebrates **National Science Day on 28 February** (Raman effect, 1928), **National Technology Day on 11 May** (Pokhran-II, 1998) and **National Mathematics Day on 22 December** (Ramanujan's birthday).

### Apex research bodies — year and parent

| Body | Year and parent |
|---|---|
| **ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research)** | 1911 (as Indian Research Fund Association) — Ministry of Health (Dept of Health Research) |
| **ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research)** | 1929 — Ministry of Agriculture (DARE) |
| **DRDO (Defence Research and Development Organisation)** | 1958 — Ministry of Defence |
| **Department of Space** | 1972 — directly under the Prime Minister |
| **Ministry of Earth Sciences** | 2006 — runs IMD, INCOIS and NCPOR |
| **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** | 1875 — Ministry of Earth Sciences |
| **Indian Science Congress Association** | 1914 — first session at Kolkata |
| **Indian National Science Academy (INSA)** | 1935 — New Delhi |
| **TIFAC (Technology Information, Forecasting and Assessment Council)** | 1988 — autonomous body under DST |
| **Vigyan Prasar (science popularisation)** | 1989 — autonomous body under DST |

### Science advisers, days and awards

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **First Principal Scientific Adviser (1999)** | A.P.J. Abdul Kalam |
| **Principal Scientific Adviser 2001–2018** | R. Chidambaram |
| **Principal Scientific Adviser appointed in April 2022** | Ajay Kumar Sood (after K. VijayRaghavan, 2018–2022) |
| **National Science Day** | 28 February — discovery of the Raman effect (1928) |
| **National Technology Day** | 11 May — Pokhran-II nuclear tests (1998) |
| **National Mathematics Day** | 22 December — Srinivasa Ramanujan's birthday |
| **Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar (from 2023)** | new national science awards — Vigyan Ratna, Vigyan Shri, Vigyan Yuva-Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar and Vigyan Team |
| **Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize** | top science prize for scientists under 45 (from 1958); now part of the Vigyan Yuva award |

## Don't confuse
- **ICMR 1911 (health) → ICAR 1929 (farming) → DRDO 1958 (defence) → ISRO 1969 (space).**
- **28 February = Science Day (Raman); 11 May = Technology Day (Pokhran-II); 22 December = Mathematics Day (Ramanujan).**
- **Kalam was the first PSA (1999)** — the PSA advises the government and does not run DST.

**Remember it:** "Health first (1911), farms next (1929), defence (1958), then space (1969)."

**TL;DR**
- ICMR 1911, ICAR 1929, DRDO 1958, Department of Space 1972, MoES 2006, IMD 1875.
- First PSA Kalam (1999); then Chidambaram (2001–18), VijayRaghavan (2018–22) and Ajay Kumar Sood (from 2022).
- The Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar (2023) brought the national science awards into one scheme: Vigyan Ratna, Shri, Yuva and Team.
keyPoints: ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research) — 1911 (as Indian Research Fund Association) — Ministry of Health (Dept of Health Research).
ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) — 1929 — Ministry of Agriculture (DARE).
First Principal Scientific Adviser (1999) — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
National Science Day — 28 February — discovery of the Raman effect (1928).

items.title: Science Schemes, Missions & Intellectual Property
items.body:
## Schemes that build talent, missions that build technology, laws that protect ideas

**In one line:** talent schemes (INSPIRE, Atal Innovation Mission, Vigyan Jyoti), technology missions (semiconductors, AI, deep ocean) and IPR laws (patents, GIs) make up the rest of India's S&T policy toolkit.

**Why it is asked:** "Atal Tinkering Labs come under?", "India Semiconductor Mission outlay", "IndiaAI Mission year", "National IPR Policy year", "term of a patent" and AP's GI products recur in APPSC and current-affairs papers.

**The story**

To draw students to science, DST launched **INSPIRE (2008)**, and **NITI Aayog** started the **Atal Innovation Mission (2016)**, which set up **Atal Tinkering Labs** in schools. Big technology bets followed: the **India Semiconductor Mission (2021)**, the **IndiaAI Mission (2024)** and the **Deep Ocean Mission (2021)**, whose crewed submersible **Matsya-6000** forms the **Samudrayaan** project. Ideas are protected by **intellectual property rights (IPR)**: the **National IPR Policy (2016)** set the slogan "Creative India; Innovative India", a **patent lasts 20 years**, and the **Geographical Indications Act (1999)** protects products tied to a place — **Darjeeling tea** was India's first GI, and AP holds GIs such as the **Tirupati laddu** and **Araku Valley coffee**.

### Talent and innovation schemes

| Scheme | Fact |
|---|---|
| **INSPIRE (Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research)** | 2008, DST — draws school and college students into science (absorbed KVPY in 2022) |
| **Atal Innovation Mission** | 2016, NITI Aayog — Atal Tinkering Labs in schools and Atal Incubation Centres |
| **Vigyan Jyoti** | DST scheme (2019) encouraging girls in Classes 9–12 to take up STEM |
| **KIRAN (now WISE-KIRAN)** | DST scheme (2014) supporting women scientists |
| **NIDHI** | DST's 2016 programme to nurture ideas and start-ups through incubators |
| **Prime Minister's Research Fellowship (PMRF)** | 2018 — PhD fellowships at IITs, IISc and other top institutions |
| **VAIBHAV fellowship** | 2023 — links Indian-origin scientists abroad with Indian institutions |

### Technology missions (beyond quantum and supercomputing)

| Mission | Year, outlay and aim |
|---|---|
| **India Semiconductor Mission** | 2021 — ₹76,000 crore for chip fabs and display units |
| **IndiaAI Mission** | March 2024 — about ₹10,372 crore for AI compute, datasets and models |
| **Deep Ocean Mission** | 2021, Ministry of Earth Sciences — Samudrayaan crewed submersible Matsya-6000 (6,000 m) |
| **National Geospatial Policy** | 2022 — opened up mapping data for Indian firms |
| **RDI Scheme approval** | approved by the Union Cabinet in July 2025; its fund is run through the ANRF |

### Intellectual property rights (IPR)

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **National IPR Policy** | May 2016 — slogan "Creative India; Innovative India"; nodal department DPIIT |
| **Term of a patent in India** | 20 years from the date of filing |
| **Patents Act** | 1970 (in force from 1972); amended in 2005 to bring in product patents |
| **Geographical Indications of Goods Act** | 1999 (in force from 2003); a GI is registered for 10 years and can be renewed |
| **India's first GI tag** | Darjeeling tea (2004) |
| **TRIPS Agreement** | WTO agreement on intellectual property (1995) |
| **Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act** | 2001 — protects plant breeders and farmers |
| **Copyright Act** | 1957 |
| **Trade Marks Act** | 1999 |

### Andhra Pradesh GI products

| GI product | What / where |
|---|---|
| **Tirupati laddu** | temple prasadam of Tirumala (GI 2009) |
| **Araku Valley Arabica coffee** | tribal coffee of the Eastern Ghats, Alluri Sitharama Raju district (GI 2019) |
| **Banganapalle mango** | mango variety of Kurnool / Nandyal region (GI 2017) |
| **Kondapalli toys** | light-wood toys of Kondapalli, NTR district |
| **Etikoppaka toys** | lacquer-coated wooden toys of Anakapalli district |
| **Srikalahasti Kalamkari** | hand-painted (pen) Kalamkari textiles of Srikalahasti |
| **Mangalagiri sarees and fabrics** | handloom cotton of Mangalagiri, Guntur district |
| **Uppada Jamdani sarees** | silk Jamdani weaving of Uppada, Kakinada district |

## Don't confuse
- **Atal Innovation Mission is under NITI Aayog**, not DST; **INSPIRE** is DST's scheme.
- **Patent = 20 years; GI registration = 10 years (renewable).**
- **Darjeeling tea** was India's first GI; **Tirupati laddu** and **Araku coffee** are AP GIs.
- **Samudrayaan / Matsya-6000** belongs to the **Deep Ocean Mission** (Ministry of Earth Sciences), not ISRO.

**Remember it:** "Patent twenty, GI ten; Creative India, Innovative India — 2016."

**TL;DR**
- INSPIRE 2008 (DST); Atal Innovation Mission 2016 (NITI Aayog); Vigyan Jyoti for girls; KIRAN for women scientists.
- Semiconductor Mission 2021 (₹76,000 crore); IndiaAI 2024; Deep Ocean Mission 2021 (Matsya-6000).
- National IPR Policy 2016; Patents Act 1970; GI Act 1999; first GI Darjeeling tea.
keyPoints: INSPIRE (Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research) — 2008, DST — draws school and college students into science (absorbed KVPY in 2022).
Atal Innovation Mission — 2016, NITI Aayog — Atal Tinkering Labs in schools and Atal Incubation Centres.
India Semiconductor Mission — 2021 — ₹76,000 crore for chip fabs and display units.
IndiaAI Mission — March 2024 — about ₹10,372 crore for AI compute, datasets and models.
National IPR Policy — May 2016 — slogan "Creative India; Innovative India"; nodal department DPIIT.
Term of a patent in India — 20 years from the date of filing.
Tirupati laddu — temple prasadam of Tirumala (GI 2009).
Araku Valley Arabica coffee — tribal coffee of the Eastern Ghats, Alluri Sitharama Raju district (GI 2019).

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — More National Institutes & the AP Science Angle
items.body:
## AP's science and research map — beyond the headline list

**In one line:** besides SHAR, NARL and the Tirupati institutes, AP hosts defence, agricultural, petroleum and central-university campuses that APPSC uses for location matching.

**Why it is asked:** AP-specific location MCQs ("NSTL is at?", "Central Tobacco Research Institute is at?", "IIITDM is at?") and the district of Sriharikota (Tirupati district since 2022) are regular APPSC items.

**The story**

**Sriharikota** island, home of SDSC-SHAR, lies in **Tirupati district** (it was in SPSR Nellore district until the 2022 reorganisation). **Visakhapatnam** is AP's defence-science city: DRDO's **Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL)** develops torpedoes and underwater weapons there, alongside **IIPE** and **IIM Visakhapatnam**. ICAR runs the **Central Tobacco Research Institute** at **Rajahmundry** and the **Indian Institute of Oil Palm Research** at **Pedavegi** (Eluru district). New central universities came with the AP Reorganisation Act: the **Central University of AP (Anantapur)** and the **Central Tribal University of AP (Vizianagaram)**.

### More AP national institutes

| Institute | Location |
|---|---|
| **Sriharikota (SDSC-SHAR)** | Tirupati district (earlier SPSR Nellore district) |
| **Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL, DRDO)** | Visakhapatnam |
| **Central Tobacco Research Institute (ICAR)** | Rajahmundry |
| **Indian Institute of Oil Palm Research (ICAR)** | Pedavegi, Eluru district |
| **IIITDM (Indian Institute of Information Technology, Design and Manufacturing)** | Kurnool |
| **IIIT Sri City** | Sri City, Tirupati district |
| **IIM Visakhapatnam** | Visakhapatnam |
| **Central University of Andhra Pradesh** | Anantapur |
| **Central Tribal University of Andhra Pradesh** | Vizianagaram |
| **Amaravati Quantum Valley** | planned around an IBM Quantum System Two (156-qubit Heron processor), with TCS and L&T |
| **Andhra University (1926)** | Visakhapatnam |
| **Sri Venkateswara University (1954)** | Tirupati |

## Don't confuse
- **NSTL (DRDO, Visakhapatnam)** builds underwater weapons. It is not ISRO and not a Navy dockyard.
- **Sriharikota is now in Tirupati district** (since 2022). Older books say Nellore.
- **IIITDM is at Kurnool; IIIT is at Sri City.**

**Remember it:** "Vizag = NSTL + IIPE + IIM; Rajahmundry = tobacco; Kurnool = IIITDM; Anantapur = Central University."

**TL;DR**
- Sriharikota is in Tirupati district; NARL is at Gadanki.
- NSTL (DRDO), IIPE and IIM are at Visakhapatnam; the Central Tobacco Research Institute is at Rajahmundry.
- Central University at Anantapur; Central Tribal University at Vizianagaram; the Amaravati Quantum Valley is built around IBM Quantum System Two.
keyPoints: Sriharikota (SDSC-SHAR) — Tirupati district (earlier SPSR Nellore district).
Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL, DRDO) — Visakhapatnam.

items.title: For Mains — S&T policy, institutions & innovation ecosystem
items.body:
**In one line**
For Mains (Paper-5, clauses M5-1 'integration of S&T, national policies, institutes in AP & India' and M5-9 'promotion of science in AP & India'), this topic is argued as *why India under-performs in research and how recent reforms try to fix it*.

**The analytical frame**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Evolution | SPR 1958 → TPS 1983 → STP 2003 → STIP 2013 → draft STIP 2020: capacity → self-reliance → investment → innovation → inclusivity |
| Strengths | large scientific workforce, strong institutions (ISRO, DRDO, CSIR), rising GII rank (38th, 2025) |
| Weaknesses / criticism | GERD only ~0.64% of GDP; government-dominated funding; weak industry-academia link; brain drain; fragmented schemes |
| Recent reforms | ANRF 2023 (apex, PM-chaired, private money), RDI Scheme 2025 (~Rs 1 lakh crore), missions (Quantum, Supercomputing, NM-ICPS), ONOS 2025 |
| AP angle | SDSC-SHAR, NARL, IIT/IISER Tirupati, IIPE, Amaravati Quantum Valley; AP's push to build an innovation cluster post-bifurcation |
| Way forward | raise GERD toward 2%, strengthen research-industry-university links, retain talent, notify STIP 2020 |

**Data, provisions and examples to quote**
- **GERD ~0.64% of GDP** vs 2% target (STIP 2003/2013) — the headline criticism.
- **ANRF Act 2023**: ~Rs 50,000 crore (2023-28), ~Rs 36,000 crore from private sources; PM is ex-officio President.
- **RDI Scheme 2025**: ~Rs 1 lakh crore corpus for private-sector R&D.
- **GII 2025**: India 38th (WIPO), tops the lower-middle-income group.
- **Article 51A(h)** anchors scientific temper as a constitutional value.
- **AP**: Amaravati Quantum Valley (IBM/TCS/L&T partners) as a state-level innovation bet.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the evolution arc (1958 → 2020) to show direction, then pivot to the GERD gap as the core problem.
- Quote ANRF and RDI figures as the 'reform' half of the answer; close with the research-industry linkage as way forward.
- Diagram idea: a funnel — policies & missions in, GERD gap in the middle, innovation outcomes (GII rank) out.
- Usable line: "India innovates above its budget — the task now is to raise the budget to match the ambition."

**TL;DR**
- Serves Mains Paper-5 (M5-1, M5-9): argue policy evolution, the GERD gap, and reforms.
- Anchor numbers: GERD ~0.64%, ANRF Rs 50,000 cr, RDI ~Rs 1 lakh crore, GII 38th (2025).
- Weaknesses: low/government-heavy funding, weak industry-academia link, brain drain.
- AP angle: Amaravati Quantum Valley and the post-2014 institute cluster.
keyPoints: Mains clauses served: M5-1 and M5-9 (mains-5) — S&T policy, institutes and promotion of science.
Core argument: policy ambition (STIP, missions) outruns financing — GERD only ~0.64% of GDP vs 2% target.
Reforms to quote: ANRF 2023 (Rs 50,000 cr), RDI Scheme 2025 (~Rs 1 lakh crore), GII 38th (2025).
Weaknesses: government-heavy funding, weak industry-academia link, brain drain, fragmented schemes.
AP angle: Amaravati Quantum Valley and the post-bifurcation institute cluster (SDSC-SHAR, IIT/IISER Tirupati).
